title: the opening
hook: the opening — seven verses said seventeen times a day
carry: in the name of the merciful

segments.voice: Yesterday: the five pillars. Five things that hold a life up, on clocks from a breath to a lifetime. Which one did you notice holding yours? Day six.
screen: `THE FIVE PILLARS — ALWAYS, DAILY, YEARLY, ONCE.`

segments.voice: Think of the thing you've said most often in your life. Your own name. Hello. Probably I'm fine. Now picture a prayer seven verses long, said seventeen times every day in the required prayers, by a child of seven and a woman of ninety, in a desert, a city apartment, an airport corner. Over a lifetime, that's hundreds of thousands of times. Whatever that prayer says, it's going to wear a groove in a person. It's called al-Fatiha. And over the next few days, we'll walk through it together, one line at a time.

Al-Fatiha means the opening. It's the first surah of the Qur'an, and its root, f-t-h, is the root of opening things: a door, a way, a city. The Arabic word for a key, miftah, grows from it too. The Qur'an speaks of seven oft-repeated verses, and many scholars read that as al-Fatiha. A hadith in Bukhari says there is no prayer without it. That's where the seventeen comes from: the five daily prayers add up to seventeen units, and every unit begins with these seven verses. Here's where we are. In the numbering printed in most copies of the Qur'an today, verse one is the line you met on day two. Pickthall: “In the name of Allah, the Beneficent, the Merciful.” On day two we opened the first half: in the name of. Today, the other half. Two names, ar-Rahman and ar-Rahim, and both come from one root, r-h-m, mercy. The Arabic word for a womb, rahim, grows from the same root. In this language, mercy has the shape of the place where you were held before you were born. Why two? Many scholars explain it like this. Ar-Rahman is mercy as wide as everything, reaching every creature, whoever they are. Ar-Rahim is mercy that stays, that keeps coming back to you in particular. So the prayer Muslims say most in their whole lives opens by naming God twice, and both names are mercy. Before power. Before judgment. Before asking for anything. That's verse one of seven. Tomorrow, we stay inside the prayer.
screen: `THE OPENING — F-T-H, A KEY.` · `NO PRAYER WITHOUT IT.` · `VERSE ONE: THE TWO MERCY NAMES.` · `R-H-M — THE ROOT OF WOMB.` · then, large: `IN THE NAME OF THE MERCIFUL.`

segments.voice: Three breaths, with the bell. The line holds two mercy names, so give each one a breath. First breath: the wide mercy. Something good that reaches everyone, sunlight, rain, the air in this breath. Second breath: the mercy that stays. Someone who kept coming back for you. Third breath, just rest. If you want, let the line go out with it: bismillah ar-rahman ar-rahim.
Al-Fatiha, line one. In the name of God, the Beneficent, the Merciful. The opening opens with mercy, twice. Sixth word.
Your line: in the name of the merciful. Today, begin one conversation that could go either way with the gentlest first sentence you have. Day six.

screen: `DAY 6 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: "MASTER OF THE DAY OF JUDGMENT."`

howItsDone: Muslims recite al-Fatiha in Arabic in every unit of every prayer, and at many other moments. When it ends in prayer, most Sunni Muslims say amin; Shia Muslims of the Ja'fari school do not say amin in the prayer.

seventeen times a day in the required prayers: it begins every unit of every prayer.
ar-Rahman and ar-Rahim come from the same root
r-h-m: mercy. the word for womb, rahim, grows from it too.
the root of fatiha also makes the Arabic word for a key
f-t-h, to open: a key is a miftah.

fork.setup: someone new to the prayer knows very little Arabic yet. which part does a hadith in Bukhari say no prayer can be without?
fork.reveal: there is no prayer without al-Fatiha. that's why it's usually among the first things a learner memorizes.

original.note: Arabic: "the opening." from f-t-h, to open, the same root as miftah, a key.

trapdoor: what you thought: the first chapter, like a preface.
what it means: the opening — seven verses said in every unit of every prayer.
what a scholar hears: the Qur'an's "seven oft-repeated" (15:87) is widely read as al-Fatiha. its first verse names mercy twice, ar-Rahman and ar-Rahim, from r-h-m, the root of "womb."

sources.quoted: In the name of Allah, the Beneficent, the Merciful.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 756; Sahih Muslim 394 (no prayer without al-Fatiha)

notes: Verse numbering: the script follows the numbering in most printed copies (Kufan count, used by Pickthall), where the bismillah is 1:1. Other counts don't number the bismillah as a verse, and the schools differ on reciting it aloud in prayer (and the Maliki school on reciting it in the obligatory prayer at all). The script doesn't go into this; a Keeper may want one sentence.

Index numbering: the index calls this 'line 1', day 7 'line 2' (whose title quotes verse 4) and day 8 'line 3' ('guide us on the straight path', verse 6). Day 7 is written to cover verses 2–4 so the 'mercy twice' carry works; as indexed, verse 5 ('Thee alone we worship; Thee alone we ask for help') has no day of its own. A Keeper should decide whether the outline gives verse 5 its own day.
'Seventeen times a day': the seventeen required units (2+4+4+3+4); travelers who shorten prayers recite fewer. Confirm.
Hadith numbers Bukhari 756 / Muslim 394 cited from memory; please confirm. The Hanafi school treats reciting al-Fatiha as required (wajib) rather than a pillar; the script only reports the hadith.
Rahman/Rahim distinction (wide mercy for all / mercy that stays with the particular) is a common scholarly explanation, one of several; confirm.
Amin after al-Fatiha: stated as most Sunni Muslims say it; Ja'fari Shia do not in prayer. Sunni schools also differ on saying it aloud or quietly. Confirm.
